By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$

$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

derivations.claim: The input matrix $K^{(0)}$ is symmetric, and for $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $v^TK^{(0)}v=\|\sum_i v_ix_i\|_2^2\ge0$. Its diagonal entries are $\|x_i\|_2^2=1$, giving the base case.

Assume the induction hypothesis that $K^{(h-1)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$, for some $1\le h<H$. By [F2]–[F3], take $G\sim N_n(0,K^{(h-1)})$; each pair $(G_i,G_j)$ has covariance $A_{ij}^{(h)}$. The growth bound $|\sigma(z)|\le|\sigma(0)|+L|z|$ and the finite Gaussian second moments make each product $\sigma(G_i)\sigma(G_j)$ integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus $K^{(h)}$ is finite and symmetric, and for every $v$, $v^TK^{(h)}v=c_\sigma\mathbb E[(\sum_i v_i\sigma(G_i))^2]\ge0$. Because $G_i\sim N(0,1)$, its diagonal is $c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]=1$ by [F5]. This establishes the induction step.

For the fixed $H$, let $P(h)$ mean that $K^{(h)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$, for $0\le h<H$. Define $Q(k)$ to mean $P(j)$ for every $j\le\min(k,H-1)$. Step 1.1 gives $Q(0)$. If $Q(k)$ and $k+1<H$, step 2.1 applied with $h=k+1$ gives $P(k+1)$ and hence $Q(k+1)$; if $k+1\ge H$, $Q(k+1)$ adds no new index. By [F6], $Q(H-1)$ holds, so $K^{(H-1)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$; when $H=1$, this is exactly the base matrix $K^{(0)}$. By [F4], take independent $G,G'$ both distributed as $N_n(0,K^{(H-1)})$. The vector with coordinates $Y_i=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\,G'_i\sigma'(G_i)$ has finite second moments; $\sigma'$ is bounded because it is the derivative of a Lipschitz differentiable function. Factoring expectations of independent variables gives $\mathbb E[Y_iY_j]=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)]=K_{ij}^{(H)}$. Therefore $K^{(H)}$ is finite and symmetric, and $v^TK^{(H)}v=\mathbb E[(\sum_i v_iY_i)^2]\ge0$ for every $v$. This proves the terminal claim and discharges the induction.

derivations.claim: Softplus is positive and nonconstant. It is analytic, has derivative in $(0,1)$, and its second derivative is at most $1/4$, so it satisfies the activation regularity assumptions. By [F2] and [F4], $\mu$ is finite; because $\sigma(Z)\ge\log 2$ when $Z\ge0$ and the standard normal density is positive on $(0,1)$, $\mu>0$. Since softplus is nonconstant, choose $z_0$ with $\sigma(z_0)\ne\mu$; continuity and the positive Gaussian density give $\mathbb E[(s-\mu)^2]>0$. Expanding this finite square and using $\mathbb E s=\mu$ yields $\mathbb E[s^2]>\mu^2$. Therefore $0<\rho<1$.

Let $U=\operatorname{span}\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$. By [F5], $\mathbb R^d=U\oplus U^\perp$, and [F6] supplies an orthonormal basis of $U^\perp$. Joining it to $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ gives the columns of an orthogonal matrix $Q$. By [F7], $W^{(1)}Q$ has the same iid Gaussian law as $W^{(1)}$, so all coordinates $W^{(1)}_{r\cdot}x_i$ are independent standard normals. Thus $\mathbb E[(\Phi\Phi^T)_{ii}]=c_\sigma\mathbb E[s^2]=1$, while for $i\ne j$, $\mathbb E[(\Phi\Phi^T)_{ij}]=c_\sigma\mu^2=\rho$. Therefore $\mathbb E[\Phi\Phi^T]=(1-\rho)I_n+\rho\mathbf1\mathbf1^T$, and its quadratic form in the unit vector $e$ is $1+(n-1)\rho$.

Conditional on the hidden weights, $e^Tu=e^T\Phi a$ is a centered normal random variable with variance $S=e^T\Phi\Phi^Te\ge0$, by [F1] and [F3]. The nonnegative random variable $S$ has expectation $1+(n-1)\rho>\rho n/2$, so the event $S>\rho n/2$ has positive probability; otherwise its expectation would be at most $\rho n/2$. On this event, for any fixed $C>0$, the conditional probability of $|e^Tu|>C\sqrt n$ is at least $P\{|Z|>C\sqrt{2/\rho}\}>0$. Averaging over the hidden weights proves positive unconditional probability, and $\|u\|_2\ge|e^Tu|$ gives the asserted absence of one confidence-uniform constant.
